newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Nov 22.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Nov 22.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- WARNINGS OVER STRONG POUND

Concern has been expressed for the competitiveness of British industry by business leaders in the wake of the sterling's rise to its highest level for about four years. Since August, the currency has gained 10 percent, making UK exports less attractive overseas and imports cheaper. The head of the Confederation of British Industry, Adair Turner, has noted that the appreciation has reached a level where it will begin affecting business levels.
-- SAFEWAY EXPANSION PLANS WILL CREATE 3,500 JOBS

UK supermarket chain Safeway has announced it intends to create about 3,500 full-time jobs over the next three years. As part of its expansion it intends to open a further 15 superstores and four smaller outlets across the country. The move will increase the total number of Safeway employees to some 50,000. The news came as the company announced a 7 percent rise in pre-tax interim profits to 228.2 million stg.
-- BANK WARNING OF TARGET GRIDLOCK

The Bank of England has warned that delays in discussions on the access to be allowed EU member states not participating in the single currency to the Target settlement system are presenting problems in tackling some of the Emu's more technical aspects. Speaking to bankers in London, a senior bank official warned that the delays in dealing with some of the more central issues of the system's operation could delay its launch and threaten its functioning once created.
-- BRITISH ENERGY IN 15-YEAR DEAL WITH SOUTHERN ELECTRIC

A deal has been secured that will involve British Energy, the nuclear group, supplying Southern Electric with power over the next 15 years. It is the first such long-term deal to be entered into ahead of the planned 1998 opening of the UK energy market to competition in the domestic supply field. British Energy has noted that the deal, being non-exclusive, will present no problems for the industry regulator Offer.
-- BAYER CHIEF CONDEMNS FAILURE TO CREATE SINGLE EU MARKET

The chairman of leading chemicals group Bayer, Manfred Schneider, speaking to a gathering of the Chemicals Industries Association in London, has sharply criticised the absence of a single European market in many areas. He noted that the range of currencies and tax systems still in operation within Europe was adding to the costs faced by businesses. He observed that a single currency was essential, warning the economic integration across the EU could not be delayed any longer.
-- GDP ESTIMATES SEND CONFLICTING SIGNALS

A series of official indicators of economic activity in the UK have indicated statistical differences that are reported to be presenting the Bank of England and the Treasury with problems with regard to accurately gauging the true state of the British economy. Over a number of successive quarters it has been observed that output has exceeded expenditure. The differences present problems in assessing inflationary pressures.
-- CBI AND TUC OPPOSE PERSONAL TAX CUTS

The Confederation of British Industry and the Trades Union Congress have been united in their appeal to the chancellor Kenneth Clarke to resist pressure to introduce cuts in personal tax levels in next week's Budget package. The head of the TUC called instead for the chancellor to concentrate on encouraging employment and investment. Kate Barker, chief economist with the CBI, warned that tax cuts would amount to a "policy error".
-- COCA-COLA ACCUSED BY BRANSON

Richard Branson, head of the Virgin group, has accused Coca- Cola & Schweppes Beverages of making use of anti-competitive sales practices against his own Virgin Cola soft drinks business unit. He particularly noted the use of sales promotions and discounts. However, analysts and a number of rivals in other small drinks companies have accused Branson of naivety, noting that Coca-Cola and its business methods had been vetted in 1991 by the Monopolies & Mergers Commission.
-- DELAYS AS CREST HIT BY LINK PROBLEM

The electronic share settlement system, Crest, has encountered more problems resulting from difficulties with a communications link between it and the Bank of Scotland, the registrar for securities using the system. The problems led to settlement of some 14 securities, including Enterprise Oil, being suspended. CrestCo, the company that runs Crest, has delayed the movement of 17 large companies away from paper-based settlement as a result of such glitches.
-- LABOUR SAYS TORIES CONSIDERED WINDFALL TAX

Government criticism of the planned windfall tax levy on privatised utilities was to some degree offset on Thursday by Labour claims that the Conservatives themselves had at one time considered such a tax. Meanwhile, the deputy leader of the Labour party, John Prescott, has denied that such a tax, if introduced, would dissuade foreign parties from investing in Britain. The government countered with claims that such a tax could lead to other countries taking retaliatory action against the UK.
